questions.why: Decreased ECF volume reduces renal perfusion pressure, stimulating renin release, which ultimately increases angiotensin II (a potent vasoconstrictor).

questions.stem: All statements about aldosterone are correct except:

options.label: A
options.text: is secreted by the adrenal cortex

options.label: B
options.text: acts on distal and collective tubules

options.label: D
options.text: increases the tubular reabsorption of K+

options.label: E
options.text: its secretion is controlled by angiotensin II

questions.why: Aldosterone increases K+ secretion (not reabsorption) in the distal nephron.

questions.stem: The secretion of renin is stimulated by:

options.label: E
options.text: increased Na+ in the tubular fluid

questions.why: Sympathetic stimulation (via beta-1 receptors on JG cells) increases renin secretion.

notes.E: High Na+ at the macula densa REDUCES renin.

questions.stem: The atrial natriuretic peptide has/have the following effect/effects:

options.label: A
options.text: increase the reabsorption of Na+ and water

options.label: B
options.text: increase the excretion of Na+ and water

questions.why: ANP causes natriuresis and diuresis (raised GFR, reduced Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct, inhibition of renin and aldosterone) and relaxes vascular smooth muscle.

questions.stem: In the juxtaglomerular apparatus are found:
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular cells have beta-1 adrenergic receptors that stimulate renin release.

questions.stem: Renin is secreted by:
questions.why: Renin is secreted by the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

notes.A: A type of nephron, not a secretory structure.
notes.E: The hypothalamus does not secrete renin.

questions.stem: Which of the following causes hyperkalemia?
questions.why: Exercise causes K+ to shift out of skeletal muscle cells, raising plasma potassium.

notes.E: β2 agonists drive K+ INTO cells.

questions.stem: Dialysis fluid used in the treatment of renal failure should contain the normal plasma levels of:
questions.why: Dialysis fluid is isotonic to plasma to prevent net fluid shifts (osmotic damage to blood cells).

notes.A: Urea should be ABSENT to remove it.
notes.E: Buffer (bicarbonate) is added to remove acid.

questions.stem: Drinking a litre of water:

options.label: E
options.text: decreases the specific gravity of the body

questions.why: Drinking water dilutes the blood, temporarily lowering plasma sodium concentration and osmolality.

questions.stem: A rise in the osmolality of extracellular fluid may lead to:

options.label: B
options.text: increased water reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubules

options.label: D
options.text: an increase in intracellular fluid volume

questions.why: Hyperosmolality is detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, triggering thirst and ADH (vasopressin) release.

notes.B: Proximal water reabsorption is not ADH-dependent.
notes.E: Not a response to raised osmolality.

questions.stem: Sodium retention:

options.label: A
options.text: occurs for several days after major surgery

questions.why: Surgery triggers aldosterone release (stress response), causing sodium retention, water retention, and potentially edema.

questions.stem: Sodium depletion differs from water depletion in that:

options.label: B
options.text: intracellular fluid volume is less affected

questions.why: In pure water depletion, fluid shifts out of cells (intracellular volume falls). In sodium depletion, ECF volume falls but ICF is relatively spared initially.

notes.D: Thirst is WORSE in water depletion.
notes.E: ADH is higher in water depletion.

questions.stem: A high blood potassium level (hyperkalaemia):

options.label: B
options.text: follows severe crush injuries to the limbs

options.label: C
options.text: may diminish cardiac performance and cause death

options.label: D
options.text: may be reduced by intravenous infusion of insulin and glucose

questions.why: Hyperkalemia is common in acute renal failure and crush injuries (cell lysis releases K+). Insulin drives K+ into cells to treat it.

notes.A: True, but so are the others.

questions.stem: A raised level of calcium in the blood (hypercalcaemia):

options.label: A
options.text: may occur when parathyroid activity decreases

options.label: B
options.text: may occur when the plasma protein level falls

options.label: C
options.text: may occur in chronic renal failure

options.label: D
options.text: increases the risk of stone formation in the urinary tract

options.label: E
options.text: causes increased excitability of nerve and muscle

questions.why: Hypercalcemia increases urinary calcium excretion, predisposing to kidney stones.

questions.stem: Thirst is stimulated by:

options.label: A
options.text: increase in plasma osmolality and volume

options.label: B
options.text: increase in plasma osmolality and decrease in volume

options.label: C
options.text: decrease in osmolality and increase in volume

options.label: D
options.text: decrease in plasma osmolality and volume

questions.why: Thirst is stimulated by cellular dehydration (high osmolality) and hypovolemia (low volume).

questions.stem: The reference interval of plasma osmolarity is:
questions.why: Normal plasma osmolality is tightly regulated between 280 and 295 mOsm/kg.

questions.stem: When the intake of water and salts is normal:

options.label: A
options.text: the osmotic pressure of ECF is higher than that of ICF

options.label: B
options.text: the osmotic pressure ICF is higher than that of ECF

options.label: C
options.text: the osmotic pressure of ECF is equal to that of ICF

options.label: D
options.text: the volume of ECF is bigger than that of ICF

questions.why: Water moves freely between compartments, so ECF and ICF are in osmotic equilibrium.

notes.D: ICF is larger (2/3 of body water).

questions.stem: All but except one are followed by thirst:
questions.why: Hypervolemia (increased blood volume) suppresses thirst, whereas the other factors stimulate it.

questions.stem: The volume of ECF is regulated by:
questions.why: ECF volume is regulated by RAAS (retains Na+), ANP (excretes Na+), and sympathetic tone (affects renal blood flow).

questions.stem: The information about the extracellular volume and its Na+ content is processed in the:
questions.why: The posterior hypothalamus is involved in regulating ECF volume and thirst.

notes.A: The lateral hypothalamus is linked to thirst and feeding.
notes.B: The anterior hypothalamus holds the osmoreceptors.

questions.stem: The acid-buffering power:

options.label: A
options.text: of HCO3- in blood is increased by respiratory control of pCO2

options.label: B
options.text: of haemoglobin exceeds that of HCO3- in blood

options.label: C
options.text: of HCO3- is increased by the action of carbonic anhydrase

options.label: D
options.text: of venous blood is normally greater than that of arterial blood

questions.why: The bicarbonate buffer system is highly effective due to respiratory control of CO2. Hemoglobin is also a major buffer, especially in venous blood.

notes.A: True, but B and D are also true.
notes.B: True, but A and D are also true.
notes.C: The enzyme speeds the reaction but does not add buffering power.
notes.D: True, but A and B are also true.

questions.stem: A drug which inhibits carbonic anhydrase:

options.label: A
options.text: decreases bicarbonate formation and reabsorption in the kidney

options.label: D
options.text: decreases urinary loss of potassium ions

questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (like acetazolamide) reduce bicarbonate reabsorption, leading to alkaline urine and metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A long-standing increase in arterial pCO2 (respiratory acidosis) leads to:

options.label: A
options.text: an increase in renal bicarbonate formation

options.label: B
options.text: a decrease in urinary ammonium salts

options.label: C
options.text: a decrease in plasma potassium concentration

options.label: D
options.text: an increase of the monohydrogen/dihydrogen phosphate ratio in urine

options.label: E
options.text: an increase in urinary bicarbonate excretion

questions.why: In chronic respiratory acidosis, the kidneys compensate by retaining/generating more bicarbonate to raise blood pH.

notes.D: The ratio FALLS (more acid in urine).

questions.stem: An acid-base buffer system:

options.label: A
options.text: can be a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base

options.label: B
options.text: can be a solution of sodium and chloride ions

options.label: C
options.text: prevents any change in pH when acid is added

options.label: D
options.text: works best when the pH is far from its pKa

questions.why: A buffer consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or vice versa) that resists changes in pH.

notes.C: Buffers MINIMISE change; they do not prevent it.
notes.D: Buffers work best near their pKa.
notes.E: Many buffers work inside cells (Hb, proteins, phosphate).

questions.stem: Acidosis in a patient may lead to:

options.label: C
options.text: a blood pH of less than 5.5

options.label: D
options.text: an urinary pH of less than 5.5

questions.why: In acidosis, the kidneys excrete excess H+ into the urine, resulting in an acidic urinary pH (often below 5.5).

questions.stem: A raised blood pH and bicarbonate level is consistent with:

options.label: D
options.text: chronic renal failure with a raised pCO2

options.label: E
options.text: a history of persistent vomiting of gastric contents

questions.why: Persistent vomiting causes severe loss of stomach acid (HCl), leading to metabolic alkalosis (high pH and bicarbonate).

notes.C: Low pCO2 with raised bicarbonate is not this picture.

questions.stem: A patient with partly compensated respiratory acidosis:

options.label: B
options.text: must have a raised bicarbonate concentration [HCO3-]

options.label: C
options.text: may have evidence of renal compensation.

options.label: D
options.text: may have respiratory failure due to hypoventilation

questions.why: Respiratory acidosis involves high pCO2 (hypoventilation). The kidneys compensate by retaining bicarbonate.

notes.A: True, but so are the others.

notes.C: True, but so are the others.
notes.D: True, but so are the others.

questions.stem: The acid-base balance is maintained by:
questions.why: Acid-base balance involves chemical buffers (immediate), respiratory compensation (fast), and renal regulation (slow but powerful).

notes.A: True, but so are the others.
notes.B: True, but so are the others.
notes.C: True, but so are the others.

questions.stem: For the buffer capacity of the blood of highest significance is the:
questions.why: The bicarbonate (hydrogen carbonate) buffer system is the most important extracellular buffer.

questions.stem: The H+ ions are excreted in the tubular fluid as a result of:
questions.why: H+ is actively secreted into the tubular lumen by the proximal and distal tubules.

questions.stem: HCO3- are excreted in the tubular fluid as a result of:
questions.why: Bicarbonate is freely filtered at the glomerulus. (Most is then reabsorbed).

notes.B: Reabsorption REMOVES it from the tubular fluid.
notes.C: HCO3- is not secreted in the proximal tubule.

questions.stem: The secretion of H+ in the tubular fluid is achieved by:
questions.why: H+ is secreted via primary active transport (H+-ATPase) and secondary active transport (Na+/H+ exchanger).

questions.stem: In acidosis, the kidneys:

options.label: A
options.text: increase the excretion of H+ and HCO3-

options.label: B
options.text: decrease the excretion of H+ and increase the reabsorption of HCO3-

options.label: C
options.text: increase the excretion of H+ and reabsorption of HCO3-

options.label: D
options.text: decrease the excretion of H+ and reabsorption of HCO3-

questions.why: In acidosis, the kidneys excrete more H+ (to remove acid) and reabsorb more HCO3- (to replenish base).

questions.stem: In alcalosis, the kidneys:

options.label: A
options.text: decrease the excretion of H+ and increase the reabsorption of HCO3-

options.label: C
options.text: increase the excretion of H+ and decrease the excretion of HCO3-

options.label: D
options.text: increase the indirect reabsorption of HCO3-

options.label: E
options.text: decrease the excretion of H+ and increase the excretion of HCO3-

questions.why: In alkalosis, the kidneys conserve H+ (decrease excretion) and excrete excess HCO3-.
